title: How picky can a grid be?
hook: A block of early adopters on a grid. Can a big enough start beat any threshold?

knows: the threshold rule q from cluster-stops-the-cascade: a person adopts once at least a share q of their neighbours have
doesNotKnow: that each network has a largest q at which a small group of early adopters can take the whole thing, and that it depends on the network's shape

misconception: Any threshold can be beaten if the starting group is big enough.
objective: The learner can explain that next to a square block on an 8-neighbour grid a newcomer sees at most 3 adopting neighbours of 8, so the block takes the whole grid at q = 3/8 and stalls above it however big it is, while on a line a newcomer sees 1 of 2, so the limit there is 1/2; this largest q is the network's cascade capacity.

claims.text: On an 8-neighbour grid a 5x5 block takes everyone at q = 3/8 (and at 1/4) and stays at 25 people at q = 2/5, 1/2 and 3/5.
claims.source: Builder's node run of the Demo.tsx simulate() on a 41 x 41 grid whose outer ring is a frozen frame (the 39 x 39 = 1,521 people inside each have 8 neighbours), synchronous rounds, 2026-10-14: q = 1/4 all 1,521 in 34 rounds; 3/8 all 1,521 in 51 rounds; 2/5, 1/2, 3/5 stay at 25. Deterministic, no randomness. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node copy of simulate() on the framed 41x41 grid: 5x5 takes 1,521 at 1/4 (34 rounds) and 3/8 (51); stays 25 at 2/5, 1/2, 3/5.

claims.text: Next to the block, a person facing the middle of a side sees 3 adopters among 8 neighbours, one near a corner sees 2, and one off a corner sees 1.
claims.source: Counting the 8 neighbours of the cells around a 5x5 block (node check 2026-10-14: 3, 2, 1). The stage draws these counts. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node neighbour counts beside a 5x5 block: side middle 3, near corner 2, off corner 1; max outside 3.

claims.text: Above 3/8 a newcomer needs 4 of 8 adopting neighbours, which nobody beside a square block has, so a 7x7 block stalls too, at 49.
claims.source: Derivation: beside a square block a non-adopter sees at most 3 adopters (the 3 cells of the side it faces), so with need 4 nobody joins and the block stays at b x b. Builder's Node run of Demo.tsx simulate() (2026-10-14): 7x7 stays at 49 at 2/5, 1/2 and 3/5. v2 quotes the 7x7 count from the learner's results table, and only if a 7x7 run above 3/8 was finished. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own independent sim (fc24/grid.mjs, own 41 x 41 framed grid): need = ceil(8q) = 4, 4, 5 at 2/5, 1/2, 3/5; 5x5 stays 25, 7x7 stays 49 (9x9 stays 81) at all three; at 1/4 and 3/8 every block takes 1,521. A cell beside a square block sees at most 3 adopters, so no block grows above 3/8. Reveal quotes the 7x7 count only if a 7x7 run above 3/8 is in the results table (survives Reset). Wording note (not a dispute): at 3/5 the need is 5, so 'needs 4' reads as 'at least 4'; the stage note at 3/5 correctly says 'they need 5'.

claims.text: On a line the two middle adopters take all 201 at q = 1/2, the q where the 5x5 grid stuck, because each newcomer sees 1 of 2 neighbours; above 1/2 no one else joins.
claims.source: Derivation: a waiting person next to the adopted run has 1 of 2 neighbours adopting, which meets q <= 1/2 and fails q > 1/2. Builder's Node run of simulate() on the 201-person line (2026-10-14): 201 at q = 1/4, 3/8, 2/5, 1/2; 2 at q = 3/5. v2: 'Line at 1/2' runs exactly this case (milestone line-half) and the results table keeps it. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own sim of the 201-person line, starters 99 and 100: 201 at q = 1/4, 3/8, 2/5, 1/2; 2 at 3/5. A waiting person next to the run sees 1 of 2 (the two end people have a single neighbour, 1 of 1, still >= q). 'Line at 1/2' runs q = 1/2 to the end and milestone line-half requires it, so cell('line', 1/2) = 201 is always in the table at reveal; ', where the grid stuck,' prints only if the 5x5 at 1/2 is recorded as stuck (25).

claims.text: That largest q is the network's cascade capacity: 1/2 for a line, 3/8 for this grid.
claims.source: Definition: the cascade capacity is the largest q at which some finite set of early adopters can spread to the whole (infinite) network. Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 19 (advanced material); S. Morris, 'Contagion', Review of Economic Studies 67 (2000). Values from the brief, supported here by the finite simulations in c1 and c4 only (the stage simulates a 1,521-person grid and a 201-person line, not infinite networks, and tries only square seeds). Attribution: fact-checker confirms; do not present 3/8 as the book's figure until a human with the book checks it. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Verified on own derivation for the infinite networks, not the book: q > 3/8 needs 4 of 8, and no cell outside a finite set's bounding box touches more than 3 cells inside it, so no finite seed spreads; at q <= 3/8 a kxk block (k>=3) fills its four side rows and then corners, giving a (k+2)x(k+2) block, so it grows forever. Same bounding-interval argument gives 1/2 for the line. Definition and E&K ch. 19, sec. 19.7 'Advanced Material: The Cascade Capacity' confirmed via web-search TOC; the book's own 3/8 figure not opened (host blocked). Morris 2000 not opened. The reveal does not attribute 3/8 to the book, so nothing learner-visible depends on the unopened text.

recall.question: On a long line, two neighbours adopt first. Each person adopts once at least a share q of their 2 neighbours has. Highest q that takes everyone?
options: Any q, with a big enough start
recall.why: Next to the adopters a newcomer sees 1 adopting neighbour of 2, however many started. So the spread works up to q = 1/2 and stops above it.
